question:
Panel: StaticText value update not appearing on/updating user interface

I'm having an issue with the holoviz panel widget StaticText. When updating it's value, the interface/webpage is not updating accordingly. Only when I click on reload page, it's pulling the updated value. I'm only facing this issue in a specific application. The background: I was looking for a discrete range slider being able to handle not only numbers but also strings. The answer given here ( https://discourse.holoviz.org/t/how-to-create-a-rangeslider-with-non-uniform-step-distance/2182/5 ) was the closest I found. Learning from the solution given there, I created a different DiscreteRangeSlider taking code from the DiscreteSlider and from the RangeSlider. It seems to work fine. Anyhow, there is one issue which I don't understand. In the following rows, I needed to do a workaround: # following line is strangely not updating view, only on reload # self._text.value = self.joined_label(*l_new) # instead: text = self._text.clone() text.value = self.joined_label(*l_new) self._composite[0] = self._text = text It was only updating the label when I clicked on reload page, when using the second row in the snippet above instead of the workaround. Can anybody explain this behaviour and solve it? Please see the complete code below. Thank you, kind regards, Jerome from bokeh.models import CustomJSTickFormatter from panel.widgets.slider import _RangeSliderBase, IntRangeSlider from panel.widgets import StaticText from panel import Column import numpy as np import param from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, Any, ClassVar from collections.abc import Mapping from bokeh.models.formatters import
reference_answer: You can trigger a watcher using .param.trigger : https://param.holoviz.org/en/docs/latest/user_guide/Dependencies_and_Watchers.html#param-trigger
llm_attempt: This usually happens because self._text is no longer the same object instance that is actually inside the rendered layout (self._composite). Panel/Bokeh only pushes an update to the browser when a parameter changes on the exact widget object whose model is embedded in the document; if something elsewhere rebuilds self._composite (or creates a fresh StaticText) without updating self._text to match, mutating self._text.value silently changes an orphaned object that is not on screen anymore, so only a full page reload (which re-renders everything from scratch) shows it. Your workaround fixes this by cloning and reassigning both self._text and self._composite[0] to the same new object, resynchronizing them. Check whether any other method in your class rebuilds self._composite or reconstructs StaticText separately, and keep a single canonical reference. As a lighter alternative, try self._text.param.trigger('value') or wrapping the update in pn.io.hold()/pn.io.unlocked() to force a push, but the real fix is eliminating the reference desync rather than working around it every time.

question:
How to export connections results in Plaxis Output with Python

I am working with tunnel segments connected by a series of connections in Plaxis. However, I am having difficulty exporting results from these connections (rotation, moment, etc.). None of the usual methods — g_o.getsingleresult , getresult , or even g_o.tabulate — seem to work. I suspect this is because this type of structure cannot be selected directly from the Plaxis Output interface and is instead accessed through the “Connection information” tab in the Project. Is there a way to automate this process? Below is a snippet of the code I am using: for name, phase in export_stages.items(): for con in cons_NB: con_name = con.Name.value rotations = g_o.getsingleresult(con, phase, g_o.ResultTypes.Connection.Rotationtot, 'Nodes',True) print(f"-{con_name} ---{rotations}")
llm_attempt: Plaxis Output's Python API mainly exposes results for objects directly selectable in Output, and connection element results (rotation, moment) generally are not reachable via getsingleresult/getresult/tabulate the same way as ordinary structural elements, since connections report per node pair rather than as one result object. Try iterating the connection's underlying nodes instead of the connection itself, e.g. g_o.getresults(con.Nodes[0], phase, g_o.ResultTypes.Connection.Rotationtot, 'node'), or check g_o.ResultTypes.Connection for node-indexed variants. Also inspect g_o.Connections (or the phase's connection collection) for a results-capable subobject distinct from the definition objects in cons_NB. If none of the standard calls work, this looks like a real gap in the scripting API for "Connection information" data - worth checking the Bentley Plaxis Python API changelog for your specific version, or asking on the Plaxis support forum, since this data type may currently require reading manually from the Output GUI or an exported report rather than direct scripting. I cannot verify the exact call without your Plaxis version's API reference.

question:
"OpenAI Python API Key Error: 'The api_key client option must be set'

I'm trying to use the OpenAI API in Python to create a chat completion, but I keep running into an error related to the API key. Here's my code: import os from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( # This is the default and can be omitted api_key=os.environ.get("OPENAI_API_KEY"), ) chat_completion = client.chat.completions.create( messages=[ { "role": "user", "content": "Say this is a test", } ], model="gpt-3.5-turbo", ) Error message: openai.OpenAIError: The api_key client option must be set either by passing api_key to the client or by setting the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable
llm_attempt: This means OPENAI_API_KEY is not actually set in the environment your Python process sees - os.environ.get('OPENAI_API_KEY') is returning None, so the client refuses to start. Fixes: 1) Set it in the same shell before running the script: on PowerShell, $env:OPENAI_API_KEY='sk-...'; on macOS/Linux, export OPENAI_API_KEY='sk-...'; then run the script from that same terminal session. 2) Or pass it directly: OpenAI(api_key='sk-...'), fine for quick testing but do not hardcode secrets in committed code. 3) If you use a .env file, it is NOT loaded automatically - install python-dotenv and call load_dotenv() before creating the client. 4) If running from an IDE (VS Code, PyCharm, Jupyter), setting the variable in a plain terminal will not affect the IDE's run configuration or kernel; set it in the IDE's own environment settings or restart the IDE/kernel after exporting it system-wide. Also double-check for typos in the variable name and that the key itself is valid and not revoked.

question:
fvcore multiple arguments forward modules?

I have a model that take more than one arguments in forward. Recently I'm trying to query some informations my model by fvcore module in python, but I can't find any document for multiple forward arguments! and edited code tried to have multiple functions: from fvcore.nn import FlopCountAnalysis, parameter_count_table def modelCount(model, input_tensor, *args, **kwargs): def _wrapped_forward(x): return model(x, *args, **kwargs) flops = FlopCountAnalysis(_wrapped_forward, input_tensor).total() params = parameter_count_table(model) return flops, params but it does not help ... I still have error.
reference_answer: Pass your multiple arguments as a single tuple . fvcore will handle it automatically. Example from fvcore.nn import FlopCountAnalysis # Your model and input tensors # model = MyModel() # tensor1 = torch.randn(1, 20) # tensor2 = torch.randn(1, 5) # Package inputs into a tuple inputs = (tensor1, tensor2) # Pass the model and the input tuple flops = FlopCountAnalysis(model, inputs).total() The tool unpacks the tuple and calls model.forward(tensor1, tensor2) internally. You don't need a wrapper.
llm_attempt: FlopCountAnalysis expects its second argument to be the actual inputs tuple matching the model's forward signature - you should not wrap the model in a plain function. Pass all positional arguments together: FlopCountAnalysis(model, (input_tensor, arg1, arg2)). Wrapping forward in a bare function like _wrapped_forward breaks it because fvcore's internals expect a real nn.Module (it likely walks named_modules() to attach per-module hooks, or traces it as a module), so handing it a plain function as the "model" raises an error (commonly an AttributeError). If some arguments must be fixed/keyword-only, write a thin nn.Module subclass whose forward hardcodes those extra args and calls the real model internally, then pass that module together with the remaining tensor inputs as a tuple to FlopCountAnalysis. In short: keep the real model object as the first argument, supply a tuple of every forward-required input as the second argument, and only wrap with a module (never a plain function) if you truly need to bind extra arguments.

question:
Python `.split()` for Bash?

With Python it's gorgeously simple, my problem is instantly solved in one method: text=''' dab a b c dab e f g dab h i j ''' print(text.split('dab')) Nevertheless, doing everything in Bash is a comfortable advantage to keep in my use case. Unfortunately, looking around it seems that there is no good way to do string splitting with multi -character delimiters on say stdout in the shell (natively or external tools). I'd be glad to be proved wrong :) [UPDATE] Sorry for not specifying this before, but the focus was on collecting in an array rather than printing.
reference_answer:
You can use GNU awk : $ awk '{printf("item %d:
%s", NR, $0)}' RS='dab
' <<EOF dab a b c dab e f g dab h i j EOF item 1: item 2: a b c item 3: e f g item 4: h i j Explanations: awk 'SCRIPT' RS='dab
' parses the input stream with dab+newline as input record separator ( RS ) instead of the default newline and applies SCRIPT to each record. The script {printf("item %d:
%s", NR, $0)} prints each record ( $0 ) to the standard output, preceded with item N:+newline where N is the record number ( awk special variable NR ). You can define a bash function, if you wish: $ my_split() { awk '{printf("item %d:
%s", NR, $0)}' RS='dab
'; } $ my_split <<EOF dab a b c dab ... EOF item 1: item 2: a ... If you want to store the items in a bash array, you can add the mapfile bash builtin, and separate the output records of awk with NUL characters (ASCII code 0) instead of the default newline. This is a common trick when items can contain newlines, as in your case. Of course, the trick works only if your input does not contain NUL characters, else you will have to use another awk output record separator. $ mapfile -d '' -t a < <(awk '1' RS='dab
' ORS='\0' <<EOF dab a b c dab e f g dab h i j EOF ) $ for((i=0; i<${#a[@]}; i++)); do printf 'item %d:
%s' "$i" "${a[i]}"; done item 0: item 1: a b c item 2: e f g item 3: h i j Explanations: The 1 awk script means "condition true (1) for all records, and apply the default action (print)" . ORS='\0' sets NUL as output record separator ( ORS ). mapfile -d '' -t a < XXX reads its standard input XXX , split it on NUL characters ( -d '' ), removes the
llm_attempt:
Bash has no built-in multi-character split, but gawk's RS (record separator) accepts a literal string, so you can replicate str.split() and load the pieces into a Bash array with mapfile:
mapfile -t parts < <(awk -v RS='dab' '{print}' <<< "$text")
Each element of parts corresponds to one chunk between occurrences of 'dab', matching Python's list.split() output (including a leading empty/whitespace-only element if the text starts with the delimiter). This needs gawk specifically - mawk/POSIX awk do not support multi-character RS. If gawk is not available, fall back to substituting the delimiter with a NUL byte and reading with mapfile -d '':
mapfile -d '' -t parts < <(sed 's/dab/\x00/g' <<< "$text")
Either way you end up with a real Bash array (access via ${parts[@]}, ${parts[0]}, etc.) instead of just printed text, which is what you said you actually need for collecting into an array.

question:
Want to convert degrees to radians and have the answer output symbolically

I am using the Sympy library in Python, and I'm trying to convert degrees to radians, and have the output rendered symbolically. Sympy does not have a function for converting degrees to radians, but the Sympy docs recommend using mpmath . I tried the following code: import mpmath as mp import sympy as sym mp.radians(126) The output is 2.19911485751286, which is correct, but computed numerically rather than symbolically. I would like it to be rendered as 0.7π (symbolic computation). The google AI guidance was convoluted and actually incorrect. Is there an easy way to do this?
reference_answer: Update: As pointed out in Oscar Benjamin's comment , sympy has a rad() function, which exactly fulfills the desired purpose. Using rad() , my original answer (see below) can be rewritten as: import sympy # Original `radians_1()` is now obsolete. # It would simply be `radians_1 = sympy.rad` def radians_2(x): # Now using `sympy.rad()` coeff, remainder = sympy.rad(x).as_coeff_Mul() return coeff.evalf() * remainder def radians_3(x): return float(x / 180) * sympy.pi # Unchanged print(sympy.rad(126)) # >>> 7*pi/10 print(radians_2(126)) # >>> 0.7*pi print(radians_3(126)) # >>> 0.7*pi I did not find rad() in the documentation of sympy 's API , which is why I used my own implementation below. However, help(sympy.rad) produces: Help on function rad in module sympy.geometry.polygon: rad(d) Return the radian value for the given degrees (pi = 180 degrees). Original answer Since the conversion is pretty straightforward, I would define a radians() function myself, using symbolic pi from sympy : import sympy def radians_1(x): return sympy.simplify(x * sympy.pi / 180) def radians_2(x): coeff, remainder = (x * sympy.pi / 180).as_coeff_Mul() return coeff.evalf() * remainder def radians_3(x): return float(x / 180) * sympy.pi print(radians_1(126)) # >>> 7*pi/10 print(radians_2(126)) # >>> 0.7*pi print(radians_3(126)) # >>> 0.7*pi Version radians_1() : Using simplify() reduces the fraction. If the fraction is not good enough already, we can go further: Version radians_2() : With as_coeff_Mul() , we split the expression into the coefficient ( 7/10 ) and the symbol ( sympy.pi ); with evalf() , we
llm_attempt:
Sympy already has this built in - you do not need mpmath at all. Use sympy.rad(), which converts degrees to radians symbolically:
import sympy as sym
sym.rad(126)  # -> 7*pi/10
This returns an exact symbolic Rational*pi expression (auto-simplified), not a float. For Unicode/pretty rendering use sym.pprint(sym.rad(126)) or sym.latex(sym.rad(126)) in a notebook. There is also sym.deg() for the inverse conversion. If your installed sympy version genuinely lacks rad/deg (very old release), the manual equivalent is sym.pi*sym.Rational(126, 180), which sympy reduces the same way. No mpmath needed - mpmath.radians always returns an arbitrary-precision float, which is exactly why you got a numeric result instead of a symbolic one; sympy's own rad/deg functions are the symbolic equivalent you are looking for.

Just to demonstrate it is there, let's take your observed hex dump: hex_dump = """5B 0A 20 20 7B 0A 20 20 20 20 22 71 75 65 73 74 69 6F 6E 49 64 22 3A 20 39 32 34 36 37 2C 0A 20 20 20 20 22 71 75 65 73 74 69 6F 6E 22 3A 20 22 49 2019 6D 20 73 6F 72 72 79 20 74 6F 20 68 65 61 72 20 74 68 61 74 20 79 6F 75 20 77 65 72 65 20 6E 6F 74 20 73 61 74 69 73 66 69 65 64 20 77 69 74 68 20 79 6F 75 72 20 5B 5B 45 4E 54 45 52 20 50 52 4F 44 55 43 54 20 4E 41 4D 45 20 48 45 52 45 5D 5D 20 2E 20 20 43 61 6E 20 79 6F 75 20 70 72 6F 76 69 64 65 20 75 73 20 73 6F 6D 65 20 64 65 74 61 69 6C 73 20 61 62 6F 75 74 20 77 68 79 20 79 6F 75 20 77 65 72 65 20 6E 6F 74 20 73 61 74 69 73 66 69 65 64 3F 22 0A 20 20 7D 0A 5D""" string_result = ''.join(chr(int(h, 16)) for h in hex_dump.split()) print(string_result) This should result in: [ { "questionId": 92467, "question": "I’m sorry to hear that you were not satisfied with your [[ENTER PRODUCT NAME HERE]] . Can you provide us some details about why you were not satisfied?" } ] If you run that through the json package we can see where your \u2019 might come from: import json string_result2 = json.dumps(json.loads(string_result), indent=4) print(string_result2) One might expect to see: [ { "questionId": 92467, "question": "I\u2019m sorry to hear that you were not satisfied with your [[ENTER PRODUCT NAME HERE]] .
llm_attempt: The bytes you show for the apostrophe (E2 80 99) are actually valid UTF-8 for U+2019, so that exact sequence should not trigger InvalidUtf8 - which suggests the real file on disk is not encoded the way your hex dump implies. A very common cause: the JSON was produced by something using Windows-1252/CP1252 (copy-pasted from Word/Excel, or saved by Notepad as "ANSI"), where the curly apostrophe is a single byte 0x92 - that lone byte is invalid as standalone UTF-8 and is exactly what Polars' strict UTF-8 JSON parser rejects. Verify the actual on-disk bytes (open the file in a hex editor, or in Python: open(path,'rb').read()) rather than trusting a retyped example. Fix by re-encoding the file to real UTF-8 before reading it, e.g. text = open('file.json', encoding='cp1252').read(); open('file_utf8.json','w',encoding='utf-8').write(text); df = pl.read_json('file_utf8.json'). Alternatively read+decode in Python's more permissive json module and build the frame with pl.DataFrame(json.loads(raw_bytes.decode('cp1252'))).

question:
Machine Learning Project using Multidimensional Array Input/Outputs

I am struggling to get my ML model to accept the input and outputs that I need. My aim is to have it accept this as the input: input_x = [ ((4.11, 8.58, -2.2), (-1.27, -8.76, 2.23)), ((0.43, -6.53, 1.25), (7.91, -10.76, 0.06)), ... ] and this as the output: output_y = [ (34,24), (13,30), ... ] The (X1,X2,X3) and the (Y1,Y2,Y3) are different measurements, but they are needed to be considered together to produce the (X, Y) output. The issue that I am running into is that LogisticRegression() does not except the multidimensional input/output. Found array with dim 3, while dim <= 2 is required by LogisticRegression So, just to get my code running, I flattened everything too: input_x = [ (4.11, 8.58, -2.2, -1.27, -8.76, 2.23) (0.43, -6.53, 1.25, 7.91, -10.76, 0.06) ... ] output_y = [ 7 -17 ... ] X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(input_x, output_y, test_size=0.4, random_state=20, shuffle=False) logreg= LogisticRegression() logreg.fit(X_train, y_train) y_pred=logreg.predict(X_test) print(f"Accuracy: {metrics.accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)}") print(f"Recall: {metrics.recall_score(y_test, y_pred, average='micro')}") print(f"Precision: {metrics.precision_score(y_test, y_pred, average='micro')}") which works, but had an accuracy of 4.5% - so here is the first round of questions: Is it possible to input data like ((X1, X2, X3), (Y1, Y2, Y3)) and output data like (X, Y) Is LogisticRegression() the right thing to use for this project, or is there something better that I should be looking at? Are there any materials/sites/resources that I should checkout? Ideally this wo
reference_answer: I don't have the final magical solution but here are my 2 cents. It is possible to map multiple inputs to multiple outputs. Flattening the input seems a good idea to me. Logistic Regression is for classification (e.g., cat vs dog), not continuous numerical outputs. That's why you get poor accuracy. What you have here is a multivariate regression problem. You can try to look into Random Forest Regression, Linear Regression, SVR, ... Sure, many scikit-learn regressors support sample_weight during training: weights = [10, 15, ...] # from your data model.fit(X_train, y_train, sample_weight=weights_train) Example: from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, r2_score # Flatten your inputs input_x = [ (4.11, 8.58, -2.2, -1.27, -8.76, 2.23), (0.43, -6.53, 1.25, 7.91, -10.76, 0.06), ] output_y = [ (34, 24), (13, 30), ] weights = [10, 15] X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, w_train, w_test = train_test_split(input_x, output_y, weights, test_size=0.4, random_state=20) model = RandomForestRegressor() model.fit(X_train, y_train, sample_weight=w_train) y_pred = model.predict(X_test) print("R2 Score:", r2_score(y_test, y_pred)) print("MSE:", mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred))
llm_attempt: scikit-learn estimators require 2D X (n_samples, n_features) and, for multi-output, a 2D y (n_samples, n_outputs) - not 3D+ arrays. Flattening X into shape (n_samples, 6) is the right move; keep doing that. But your targets look like continuous coordinates, (34,24), (13,30), not discrete classes, so this is really a multi-output regression problem, not classification - which is why LogisticRegression gives near-random "accuracy": accuracy/precision/recall are the wrong metrics for continuous targets. Keep y two-dimensional instead of collapsing it to one number: y = np.array([[34,24],[13,30], ...]). Then use a regressor with native or wrapped multi-output support, e.g. sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression, RandomForestRegressor, or sklearn.multioutput.MultiOutputRegressor(SomeRegressor()) if the base estimator does not support multi-output directly. Evaluate with mean_squared_error/r2_score per output instead of accuracy. If (X,Y) are actually categorical bins rather than continuous measurements, use MultiOutputClassifier instead - but given the values shown, regression is almost certainly what you want.

question:
How to render raw html in the PyHTML library I am not able to render a table generated by the pandas .tohtml() function into my pyhtml generated code. s = h.html( h.head( h.title("Student Data") ), h.body( h.h1( "Student Details" ), (sdf.to_html(index=False)) ) ) This is what I tried, ends up giving me the table as a string. Heard about a raw() method, but the current version just says its not existent.
Student id Course id Marks
1002 2001 67
This is the approx structure of my html table
reference_answer:
Be careful though! PyHTML escapes these sequences for good reason, so don't do this unless you have a very good reason, and are certain that your text is trusted. You can enclose the output from sdf.to_html() in div or span tag and pass _safe=True , e.g. import pyhtml as h from pandas import DataFrame sdf = DataFrame(data = {'Student id': [1002], 'Course id': [2001], 'Marks':[67]}) s = h.html( h.head( h.title("Student Data") ), h.body( h.h1( "Student Details" ), h.div(sdf.to_html(index=False), _safe=True)) ) print(s.render()) output: Student Data

Student Details

Student id Course id Marks
1002 2001 67
Alternatively, you can use pyhtml-enhanced package instead. There is DangerousRawHtml . See Embedding raw HTML import pyhtml as h from pandas import DataFrame sdf = DataFrame(data = {'Student id': [1002], 'Course id': [2001], 'Marks':[67]}) s = h.html( h.head( h.title("Student Data") ), h.body( h.h1( "Student Details" ), h.DangerousRawHtml(sdf.to_html(index=False)) ) ) print(s.render())
llm_attempt: pyhtml escapes any string you pass as a child, which is why the table shows up as literal markup text - that is expected safety behavior, not a bug. If raw()/Raw() does not exist in the version you have installed, check that version's source or changelog for the current name of its "unsafe/do-not-escape" node type - implementations vary and some rename it (e.g. Markup, NotEscaped, or a str subclass the renderer skips). As a fallback that works regardless of the library's exact API, render the skeleton with pyhtml normally, then splice the table HTML into the final string yourself instead of inside the DSL tree: build shell = h.html(h.head(h.title('Student Data')), h.body(h.h1('Student Details'), '__TABLE__')), then page = str(shell).replace('__TABLE__', sdf.to_html(index=False)). Or skip the DSL for that one node and assemble the final HTML with an f-string around sdf.to_html(index=False) directly. This guarantees the table is inserted unescaped without depending on whichever raw-HTML helper your specific pyhtml version happens to support.

question:
Pylance in devcontainer is loading forever

I am trying to set up a devcontainer on my desktop, but functions like autocomplete or go to function don't work. When I hover variable or function it shows never-ending load information Loading information . I was trying use different Pylance versions and different images but results were the same. When RAM hits the threshold of 6.5GB, then it suddenly decrease to 2.5GB and Pylance switch port to a different one. This cycle repeats infinitely. Also, I got this message Enumeration of workspace even if workspace directory contains only test file like this. test = 'test' print(test) Notebooks and files are executing normally. I was using Pylance 2025.7.1, VS Code 1.102.3, Docker 4.43.1 with WSL 2.5.9.0 and Windows 11. Dockerfile FROM pytorch/pytorch:2.7.1-cuda12.8-cudnn9-devel RUN apt-get update && apt-get upgrade -y RUN apt-get -y install git RUN pip install jupyter ipykernel packaging ninja mlflow tqdm torchinfo matplotlib RUN pip install flash-attn --no-build-isolation RUN pip install "unsloth[cu128-torch271] @ git+https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth.git" RUN pip install triton --extra-index-url "https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128" Docker-compose.yaml services: pytorch: container_name: pytorch build: context: . dockerfile: Dockerfile ports: - "8888:8888" environment: - JUPYTER_TOKEN=easy working_dir: / volumes: - ../:/workspace deploy: resources: reservations: devices: - driver: nvidia capabilities
reference_answer: Restrict your workspace to just the folder you actually care about. Change your devcontainer.json so that VS Code’s workspace is /workspace (location of the ode), not / .

Creation of large Numpy tables with broadcasting - how to speed-up

In a python code, I need to compute a huge 4-D table of ~5000x50x100x100 elements. It contains a normal distribution whose parameters span the different dimensions, and the creation essentially reads like : result = gaussian( val[np.newaxis, :, np.newaxis, np.newaxis], mean[:, np.newaxis, :, :], sigma[:, np.newaxis, np.newaxis, np.newaxis] ) Where gaussian is obviously : def gaussian(x, mu, sigma): return np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - mu) / sigma) ** 2) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi ) / sigma The sole creation of this table takes very long and slows down the code significantly. Is there any obvious way to speed-up this step ?

Quick wins: 1) Use float32 instead of float64 to halve memory bandwidth if precision allows. 2) Use numexpr, which evaluates the whole expression in one fused, multithreaded pass without materializing every intermediate: import numexpr as ne; ne.evaluate("exp(-0.5*((x-mu)/sigma)**2)/(sqrt(2*pi)*sigma)"). This alone often gives a large speedup on exactly this pattern. 3) Or write it with numba's @njit(parallel=True) and explicit loops to avoid temporaries entirely. 4) If a GPU is available, cupy is a near drop-in replacement for numpy and this embarrassingly parallel elementwise workload will run much faster on it. 5) Precompute 1/sqrt(2*pi) once. Also consider whether you need the full dense array at once, or can stream/chunk it to cut peak memory.

question:
Automatic Data Sending

I am working on a project that uses python. It is a mmWave board that is used to collect vital sign data. I am creating logs of the vital sign data and it saves as an excel sheet. How to automatically use the Excel sheet data to create a graph each time I close the application that collects the data? And then when this graph is generated, how to display it after automatically?
reference_answer: if you put application that collects the data and program which creates graph in one script (bash/bat/etc.) then this script first will run application for data, and after closing this aplication it will run automatically next program (which creates graph). If it is a plain script, register with atexit: atexit.register(make_graph) runs make_graph() on normal interpreter exit. If it is a GUI app (e.g. Tkinter), bind the window's close event instead, since atexit does not reliably fire on abrupt GUI termination: root.protocol('WM_DELETE_WINDOW', on_close), where on_close() builds the graph then destroys the window. If your data-collection app already has its own exit hook or callback system, prefer that over atexit for reliability.

question:
Does `.all()` in Django re-query the Database or use the cache?

I am getting very conflicting messages. From Django Queryset docs, I am reading ( https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.1/ref/models/querysets/#django.db.models.query.QuerySet.all ): When a QuerySet is evaluated, it typically caches its results. If the data in the database might have changed since a QuerySet was evaluated, you can get updated results for the same query by calling all() on a previously evaluated QuerySet. But then under the prefetch_related section, it shows that using .all() on the sub-objects uses results from the cache: >>> restaurants = Restaurant.objects.prefetch_related( ... Prefetch("pizzas", queryset=queryset), ... ) >>> vegetarian_pizzas = restaurants[0].pizzas.all() Here, apparently vegetarian_pizzas doesn't trigger a database query. So...which is it - what does all() actually do? Why does it trigger a database query on the outer but then not for sub-objects? I'm confused.
reference_answer: Here, apparently vegetarian_pizzas doesn't trigger a database query. QuerySet s itself don't trigger queries. QuerySet s are lazy, this means that only if you enumerate, call str(…) or len(…) on it, or anything else that actually needs the data it will make a query. A QuerySet also caches the result once a query is made, such that enumerate over it a second time, will not query the database a second time. Now .all() [Django-doc] makes a clone of the QuerySet , and that clone thus has a different cache, this thus means that if you call .all() and then you evaluate the original queryset, it will cache the results in the original queryset, but not in its .all() clone. So: qs 1 = my_queryset qs 2 = qs 1 .all() print(qs 1 ) print(qs 2 ) will make two queries. The confusion probably stems from the fact that .all() also has an extra use-case when you are working with a manager . You can not enumerate over a manager, like my_restaurant .pizzas , it thus is used as a tool to get the underlying QuerySet by using .all() . Indeed, if we look at the source code [GitHub] : def all(self): # We can't proxy this method through the `QuerySet` like we do for the # rest of the `QuerySet` methods. This is because `QuerySet.all()` # works by creating a "copy" of the current queryset and in making said # copy, all the cached `prefetch_related` lookups are lost. See the # implementation of `RelatedManager.get_queryset()` for a better # understanding of how this comes into play. return self.get_queryset() So to summarize, .all() makes a clone if we are working with a QuerySet . But here we work wit
llm_attempt: Both statements are true, they just apply to different objects. Model.objects.all() called on a manager always returns a brand-new, unevaluated QuerySet - no caching involved yet. Calling .all() on an already-evaluated QuerySet instance (not the manager) clones it into a fresh QuerySet without carrying over the old result cache, so evaluating that clone re-hits the database - that is the "get updated results" behavior the first doc excerpt describes. The prefetch_related case is a deliberate special case: prefetching populates a private _prefetched_objects_cache on the related manager, and calling .all() on that specific related manager (e.g. restaurant.pizzas.all()) checks for that cache first and returns it directly instead of cloning and querying, so that calling .all() does not silently defeat the point of prefetching. So: plain .all() on an evaluated queryset = fresh clone = queries again on next evaluation; .all() on a prefetched relation's manager = intentionally cache-aware and skips the query. It is not inconsistent, just two different code paths with different rules.

I tried a bunch of solutions, the most obvious of which is asyncio tasks: # Data source DataSource = Generator[int, Any, None] def create_data_source() -> DataSource ... # Data processing - should be able to run in the background until being shut down async def data_processor(source: DataSource) -> None: try: for item in source: print("Working") except Exception as e: print("Exception", e) raise finally: print("Cancelled") async def main(): # Run the function data_source = create_data_source() processing_task = asyncio.create_task(data_processor(data_source)) # Do other stuff await asyncio.sleep(3) # Shut the function down processing_task.cancel() asyncio.run(main()) The problem is - once the task starts, the "Working" loop never terminates. I tried making the loop async, I tried sending it a shutdown signal using asyncio.Event , and I even tried rewriting the function using concurrent.futures , but nothing works. What am I missing? You should consider running it as a sync function using run_in_executor using either a thread pool (the default) or a multiprocessing pool created with concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor according to its CPU usage. For example: Using a Multithreading Pool import asyncio import time from threading import Event # Data processing - should be able to run in the background until being shut down def data_processor(stop_event) -> None: start_time = time.time() try: while True: if stop_event.is_set(): break print("Working") except Exception as e: print("Exception", e) raise finally: print(f"Started at {start_time}, ended at {time.time()}") async def main(): stop_event = Event() # We don't need a larger pool: loop = asyncio.get_running_loop() awaitable = loop.run_in_executor(None, data_processor, stop_event) # Do other stuff await asyncio.sleep(3) # Shut the function down stop_event.set() await awaitable # Wait for task to complete if __name__ == '__main__': asyncio.run(main()) Prints: Working Working ... Working Started at 1738589602.7931993, ended at 1738589605.79333 Using a Multiprocessing Pool Here we cannot directly pass a multiprocessing.Event instance to the worker function and must instead use a pool initializer to initialize each pool process with a global reference to the event: import asyncio import time from multiprocessing import Event from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor def init_pool(_stop_event: Event) -> None: global s
llm_attempt:
Cancellation only takes effect at an await suspension point. Your for loop over source never awaits, so the task never yields back to the event loop - the cancellation request has nowhere to be delivered until the loop finishes, and if source is effectively infinite it also likely starves your asyncio.sleep(3) in main from ever getting to run concurrently in the first place. Fix by adding an await checkpoint inside the loop:

    print("Working")
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
That yields control each iteration and is where CancelledError actually gets raised once cancel() is called. Your existing except Exception will not swallow it - CancelledError is a BaseException subclass since Python 3.8, so it still propagates to your finally block as written. If source is a blocking/CPU-bound generator that genuinely cannot await anything, run it in a thread via loop.run_in_executor and signal cancellation with a threading.Event instead, since real OS-thread work cannot be interrupted by asyncio.Task.cancel().

question:
How can I make all attributes in a Python dataclass optional without rewriting each one?

I have this data class: @dataclass class User: id: str name: str pwd: str picture: str url: str age: int # many, many more attributes Now, I have to make all of the attributes of my data class optional because of a change in the data I am receiving. I know I can do something like this: @dataclass class User: id: Optional[str] = None name: Optional[str] = None # and so on for the 25-30 attributes I have But is there a more efficient way to accomplish this without having to manually write Optional[..] = None for every line? For example, I used to get data like: attributes = {"id": "18ut2", "pwd": "qwerty", "name": "John Doe", "picture": None, "age": None, "url": "www.example.com"} user = User(**attributes) Before, if the attribute was None , the key was not omitted. Unlike now, when a key is None , the entire key is omitted. Example of current data: attributes = {"id": "18ut2", "pwd": "qwerty", "name": "John Doe", "url": "www.example.com"} # No picture or age key anymore user = User(**attributes) # Now throws an error Error: TypeError: User.__init__() missing 2 required positional arguments: 'picture' and 'age' Note: I know overriding __init__ or using __init_subclass__ , but those come with limitations, so I am looking for a solution that avoids that.
reference_answer: Here's a class decorator that will transform the class attributes to optional before processing with dataclass , and an example of usage. The example assumes this code is in optional_dataclass.py : class _NO_DEFAULT: pass NO_DEFAULT = _NO_DEFAULT() def all_fields_optional(cls): """Mark all valueless annotated fields in a class as optional. Used for dataclasses. This decorator must come _after_ the `@dataclass` decorator in the list of class decorators. Example: @dataclass @all_fields_optional class SimplePerson: name: str age: int """ for field, f_type in getattr(cls, '__annotations__', {}).items(): if getattr(cls, field, NO_DEFAULT) == NO_DEFAULT: if isinstance(f_type, str): cls.__annotations__[field] = f_type + '|None' else: cls.__annotations__[field] = f_type | None setattr(cls, field, None) return cls This code looks at all the class annotations. For each annotation, if the named class attribute has no defined value, it modifies the annotation to allow for None and sets the class attribute to None . from dataclasses import dataclass from optional_dataclass import all_fields_optional @dataclass @all_fields_optional class SimplePerson: name: str age: int anne = SimplePerson('Anne', 10) annie = SimplePerson('Annie') anon = SimplePerson() print(repr(anne)) print(repr(annie)) print(repr(anon)) output: SimplePerson(name='Anne', age=10) SimplePerson(name='Annie', age=None) SimplePerson(name=None, age=None)
llm_attempt:
There is no built-in one-liner to make an existing @dataclass's fields all Optional without touching each annotation, because @dataclass generates __init__ at class-definition time directly from the annotations and defaults present. The practical fix that avoids rewriting 30 fields is to not change the class at all - instead merge a full None-defaults dict with your possibly-partial incoming data before constructing:
import dataclasses
defaults = {f.name: None for f in dataclasses.fields(User)}
user = User(**{**defaults, **attributes})
This makes any missing key default to None no matter how many fields you add later, with zero changes to User itself. If you want it enforced on the class, write a small decorator that runs after @dataclass and rebuilds __init__, or switch to pydantic's BaseModel, where Optional[...] = None per field is still explicit but partial construction and validation are more first-class. There is no "all_optional=True" flag on the standard library dataclass decorator itself.
